Pool Service in Buckeye, AZ, a City That Runs on Well Water

Every drop the City of Buckeye delivers is pumped from the ground, and that well water is what fills and tops off your pool. Call the free line any hour to be put through to an independent, locally owned pool company that works in Buckeye.

Pool service in Buckeye, AZ deals with water that has spent a long time underground. The city pumps all of the water it delivers from wells, and that groundwater carries a heavy load of natural minerals into every pool it fills. This page covers how that mineral load shapes pool care here, and how a single free phone call puts you in touch with a nearby pool company.

Buckeye: a city that pumps all of its own water

The City of Buckeye's water utility relies on groundwater alone for the water it delivers. The city reports roughly 11,970 acre-feet a year of drinking water, about 3.9 billion gallons, coming from 33 active wells. Local reporting describes the Hassayampa sub-basin, which sits under much of Buckeye's planning area, as the source of all of it. The city does hold allocations of Colorado River water, but most of that goes into the ground to recharge the aquifer rather than straight to taps.

Not every Buckeye home is on city water. The city lists three providers inside Buckeye: its own Water Resources Department, EPCOR Water and Arizona Water Company. Which one serves you depends on the address, and the name is on your water bill. That matters for a pool, because each provider publishes its own water quality report and its own rules.

What Buckeye's groundwater does to a pool

The city says the minerals that occur naturally in its well water, typically calcium, sodium and magnesium, are not pleasing to customers for smell, taste and hardness. A pool feels that load more than a kitchen tap does.

Total dissolved solids

Total dissolved solids, or TDS, is the total amount of minerals and salts dissolved in water. The EPA treats it as an aesthetic matter with only a secondary guideline, not a health limit, and Buckeye's water meets federal standards. In a pool, TDS only climbs as water evaporates.

Calcium and scale

Calcium hardness is the amount of dissolved calcium in the water. When it runs high, it can come out of solution as white or gray scale on tile, in heaters and inside salt cells, which is why it is worth testing in the pool itself.

Wells chosen with care

The city says much of the local groundwater is poor quality and would be costly to treat, so it has worked to place its wells in areas with better water. That keeps tap water acceptable, but it does not make it soft.

A tight water supply and your pool

Water planning is a live issue in Buckeye. In January 2023 a state groundwater model found the Lower Hassayampa sub-basin about 15 percent short of the water needed to meet Arizona's 100-year assured water supply test, and the city published a response. Buckeye says it has the water to serve existing customers and the growth that already holds certificates of assured water supply, and it has been adding sources. City leaders approved spending about $80 million on groundwater rights in the Harquahala area that allow the city to pump 5,926 acre-feet a year for 100 years.

Nearly all homes in the city also belong to the Central Arizona Groundwater Replenishment District, which uses member fees to buy other water supplies and put water back into the ground for what the city pumps. None of this limits normal pool use, but it is a good reason not to waste water. A slow leak, a filler valve that sticks or a drain that was not needed all waste groundwater.

Safe checks before you call

  • Waterline. Look for white or gray crust on the tile and note how far the water has dropped at the skimmer.
  • Baskets. Empty the skimmer and pump baskets, which fill quickly after windy days.
  • Filter gauge. Write down the pressure reading so the company can compare it with a clean filter.
  • Equipment pad. Check for drips or damp ground around the pump, filter and pipes.
  • Breaker. Reset a tripped breaker or GFCI once. If it trips again, leave it off and call.

Safety first. Never mix pool chemicals with each other. Keep them apart, dry, shaded and out of children's reach, and follow the label. Keep children away from a pool without a fence or cover, and treat a green or murky pool as a drowning hazard since no one can see the bottom. If you smell gas near a pool heater, leave the area, do not touch switches or the heater, and from a safe distance call 911 or the emergency number on your gas bill.

Reading your provider's report, and questions to ask

The City of Buckeye posts its Annual Water Quality Report on its Environmental Compliance page. The current one covers tests from January 1 through December 31, 2024. If EPCOR Water or Arizona Water Company serves your home, read that provider's report instead. Look for the mineral rows, such as hardness and TDS, then compare them with your own pool test over a few months. For power, check the utility named on your bill; it handles outages, not pool equipment. Before draining, read how often to drain a pool in Arizona.

Questions to ask a Buckeye pool company

  • What is your Arizona ROC license number? Needed for repair, equipment and resurfacing work. Check it on the ROC search yourself.
  • Do you test TDS as well as calcium? With well water, both numbers tell you where the pool is heading.
  • How do you keep scale off the tile and out of the heater or salt cell? Ask what the plan is, not just the price.
  • If draining is needed, how much and where does it go? A partial drain may be enough and uses less water.
  • What is on the written quote? Labor, parts and chemicals, listed before work starts.

Common questions

Where does Buckeye AZ get its water?

For homes on city water, from wells. The City of Buckeye says groundwater is its only delivered supply, pumped from 33 active wells, and the Hassayampa sub-basin under much of the city's planning area is where it comes from. The city also holds Colorado River water, but most of it is used to recharge the aquifer, and reclaimed water goes to uses such as landscaping. Some Buckeye addresses are served by EPCOR Water or Arizona Water Company instead, so check the name on your water bill.

Why does Buckeye water leave white spots and crust on my pool tile?

Buckeye's groundwater carries naturally dissolved minerals, mainly calcium, sodium and magnesium, which the city describes as total dissolved solids. When pool water evaporates those minerals stay behind, and each top off adds more. Over time they show up as crust at the waterline and on the tile.

Who is my water provider in Buckeye?

It depends on where you live. The city lists three providers within Buckeye: the city's own Water Resources Department, EPCOR Water and Arizona Water Company. Your water bill shows which one serves your address, and that provider's annual water quality report is the one to read.

Should I drain my pool in Buckeye because of hard water?

Not before the water is tested. A pool company can test calcium hardness and total dissolved solids and tell you whether a partial drain, a full drain or neither makes sense. Ask where the water will go, and keep in mind that refill water comes from the same wells.

Do I need a licensed company for pool repairs in Buckeye?

Routine cleaning and chemical care are generally not treated as contracting. Repairs, equipment replacement and resurfacing generally call for a contractor licensed by the Arizona Registrar of Contractors. Ask for the ROC license number and check it on the ROC contractor search.
